title: Abd al-Rahman III
hook: who declared a caliphate in Cordoba

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mosque of Cordoba: red-and-white arches in every direction, and every row facing one wall. Your line was: a forest of arches. What did you face for a full minute? Day nine hundred thirty-six.

A story is told in the later histories of al-Andalus. When a great ruler of Cordoba died, after a long reign of victories, building and wealth, a note was found among his things in his own hand. On it he had counted the days of his life when he had been truly happy, free of worry. There were only a handful. Whether it happened exactly that way, nobody can say for certain. But it's told about this man for a reason: he had everything a ruler could want, and the story says it wasn't enough. His name was Abd al-Rahman III.
screen: `A NOTE FOUND AFTER HIS DEATH.` → `ONLY A HANDFUL OF HAPPY DAYS.` → `A RULER WHO HAD EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: He came to power young, over a land in pieces. Rebels held fortresses in the hills, and cities obeyed when it suited them. He spent years in the saddle bringing them back under Cordoba's rule. Then he did something bold. Rulers of al-Andalus before him had called themselves emir, prince. He took the title caliph, and commander of the faithful. Why? In Baghdad, the Abbasid caliph had grown weak. In North Africa, the Fatimids had declared a caliphate of their own, led by Isma'ili Shia imams. Abd al-Rahman answered by claiming the title for Cordoba. Now there was a caliph in the east, a caliph in North Africa, and a caliph in the far west, all at once. For Sunni Muslims, a caliph is the successor who leads the community; Shia Muslims hold that rightful leadership belongs to the Imams of the Prophet's family. The title meant different things depending on who was asking. Under him Cordoba flourished. He built a palace city outside it, Madinat al-Zahra, with halls of marble and gardens. Envoys came from distant kings. A Jewish physician, Hasdai ibn Shaprut, served at his court. But a golden age has a bill. Armies, taxes, campaigns against neighbors, enslaved servants and soldiers in the palace. Later, under his descendants, the caliphate broke apart in civil war, and the palace city was looted and left in ruins. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory." A western caliphate.
screen: `FROM EMIR TO CALIPH.` · `THREE CALIPHS AT ONCE.` · `MADINAT AL-ZAHRA RISES.` · `A GOLDEN AGE HAS A BILL.` · then, large: `A WESTERN CALIPHATE.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about a golden age's cost. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a time that people call golden: in history, in a company, in a family, maybe in your own life. Remember what was good about it, really good. Then ask, gently: who paid for it? Whose work, whose taxes, whose quiet suffering held it up, and who doesn't appear in the story? You don't have to decide it wasn't golden. Just hold the light and the bill side by side. If you pray, you can remember the ones who paid. If you don't, just keep them in view for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Abd al-Rahman III. The ruler of Cordoba who took the title caliph, built Madinat al-Zahra, and, the story says, counted only a handful of happy days. Today's word.
Your line: a western caliphate. Today, when something shines, a product, a party, a plan, ask once who is paying for it. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: The caliphate of Cordoba is remembered in Muslim histories as part of al-Andalus's story of learning and building, and visitors today can walk the excavated ruins of Madinat al-Zahra near Cordoba.

original.note: Arabic: caliph, a successor or deputy; the title Abd al-Rahman III took.

trapdoor: what you thought: a caliph is a kind of king, and there was always just one.
what it means: Abd al-Rahman III claimed the title in Cordoba while rival caliphs ruled in Baghdad and North Africa.
what a scholar hears: khalifa, successor, a word Sunni and Shia Muslims understand differently, and a claim made partly in answer to the Fatimids.
